title: Baizhang's fox
hook: an old man was reborn a fox for saying the awakened are free of cause and effect (Gateless Gate 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: wash your bowl, and your line, wash your bowl. Did one small thing get finished all the way? Day two hundred eighty, the end of the week.

Every time the teacher Baizhang gave a talk, an old man stood at the back with the monks and listened. When the talk ended, he left with them. Nobody seemed to know him. One day, when everyone else had gone, the old man stayed behind. Baizhang asked him: who are you? And the old man said: I'm not a human being. This is the second case of the Gateless Gate, and it's the closest thing Zen has to a ghost story. It's also about one of the oldest temptations in spiritual life: thinking you've gotten past the rules.
screen: `AN OLD MAN AT THE BACK.` → `WHO ARE YOU?` → `I'M NOT A HUMAN BEING.`

segments.voice: The old man tells his story. Long ago, in the time of a Buddha before ours, I lived on this mountain as its teacher. A student asked me: does a person of great practice still fall under cause and effect? I answered: no, they don't fall under cause and effect. And for that answer I was reborn as a fox, five hundred lifetimes in a row. Please, give me a turning word, a phrase that can set me free. Baizhang said: they are not blind to cause and effect. In Chinese the difference is one character. The old man had said bù luò, doesn't fall into. Baizhang said bù mèi, isn't blind to, doesn't obscure. At that, the story says, the old man woke up. He bowed and asked Baizhang to give him a monk's funeral, behind the mountain. After the meal Baizhang called the monks to a funeral, and they were baffled, since no one was sick. He led them to a rock behind the mountain, drew out a dead fox with his staff, and cremated it with full rites. Here's the teaching. The old man thought awakening would lift him above cause and effect, the way some people imagine a spiritual person is beyond ordinary consequences. Baizhang's answer: no one is above it. Awakening means seeing it clearly. Look back at this week. No walls, no fear. Gone beyond. Form is emptiness. Don't solve it. Mu. Wash your bowl. And now: even the wisest are not blind to cause.
screen: `AN OLD TEACHER'S WRONG ANSWER.` · `FIVE HUNDRED LIVES AS A FOX.` · `NOT FALL, BUT NOT BLIND.` · `A MONK'S FUNERAL FOR A FOX.` · then, large: `NOT BLIND TO CAUSE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one small cause and its effect from today. A late night and a heavy morning. A kind word and a softer face across the table. Look at it plainly, without blame, the way you'd watch one domino tip the next. Then notice the breath: the in-breath causes the out-breath, and the out-breath makes room for the next in-breath. Watch the chain, link by link. The bell holds the time.
Baizhang's fox. An old teacher said the awakened don't fall under cause and effect, and lived five hundred lives as a fox until he heard: they aren't blind to it.
Your line: not blind to cause. Today, before one choice, take a breath to see where it leads. Day two hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Zen teachers use Baizhang's fox to warn students against thinking insight puts them beyond ethics and consequences; Baizhang himself is remembered for writing rules for monastic life.

fork.setup: a student asks you: once someone is fully awake, are they still under cause and effect? you're Baizhang. what's the turning word?
options: they aren't blind to cause and effect.
cause and effect is only an idea.
fork.reveal: Baizhang's 'bù mèi yīnguǒ' freed the old man: awakening doesn't lift anyone above consequences, it sees them clearly.

original.note: Chinese bù mèi yīnguǒ: not blind to cause and effect, Baizhang's turning word.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's a fairy tale about a man turned into a fox.
what it means: no one, however awake, is above cause and effect; awakening sees it clearly.
what a scholar hears: the case turns on one character, luò (fall) versus mèi (be blind to), and foxes in Chinese folklore are shape-shifters, apt for a teacher who took on a false form.

notes: Case 2 paraphrased; the Huangbo coda (he slaps Baizhang) is left out for length.
'In the time of a Buddha before ours': the case names Kashyapa Buddha; confirm.
Trapdoor fox-folklore note is the writer's context: confirm or trim.
Baizhang's association with the first Chan monastic rules (Baizhang qinggui) is traditional; later scholarship questions it.
